label: Yirmeyahu (Jeremiah) — Part 5 — Chapters 32–39
summary_plain: While Yerushalayim is under Babylonian siege, YHWH tells Yirmeyahu to buy a field in Anatot — a sign that houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land. YHWH promises to gather the people from all the countries where he has driven them and bring them back. Yirmeyahu speaks against Tsidqiyahu the king. The officials throw Yirmeyahu into the cistern of Malkiyahu — he sinks in the mud. Ebed-Melek the Cushite, a court official, goes to the king and says: These men have done evil by putting the prophet in the cistern. Ebed-Melek takes thirty men, pulls Yirmeyahu out with ropes and rags. YHWH promises Ebed-Melek: I will deliver you on that day — you shall not be given into the hand of the men you fear — because you have put your trust in me.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the DSS Jeremiah manuscripts (4QJer-a through 4QJer-e) and the Orit Ge'ez. Ebed-Melek the Cushite (chapters 38-39) is among the most significant figures in the prophetic literature — an African court official who rescues the prophet of YHWH and receives a personal divine promise of protection. His identity is textually confirmed: 'Ebed-Melek the Cushite' — Cushite meaning from the land of Cush (Nubia/Ethiopia). He operates at the highest level of the Judean royal court during the final siege. YHWH's specific promise to him (39:15-18) makes Ebed-Melek one of the few individuals in the prophetic corpus to receive a named, personal covenant guarantee. The field purchase at Anatot (chapter 32) is YHWH's sign of future restoration — performed during the destruction itself.

key_terms.definition: While imprisoned during the Babylonian siege, Yirmeyahu buys his cousin Khanamel's field at Anatot as a sign: 'Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.' The act of purchase during a siege is a prophetic act of hope.
Yirmeyahu has two copies of the field purchase deed — one sealed, one open — stored in an earthen jar as a sign that records will survive: land transactions will resume in Yehudah after the exile.
Yirmeyahu 33:15-16 repeats and expands the Righteous Branch promise from 23:5-6; both Yehudah and Yerushalayim will be saved; the city itself is named 'YHWH Our Righteousness.'

key_terms.term: Covenant as Sure as Night and Day
key_terms.definition: YHWH declares the Davidic covenant and the Levitical covenant as sure as his covenant with day and night — 'as long as night and day continue, so the seed of David will have a descendant to reign.'

The last king of Yehudah; Yirmeyahu repeatedly counsels him to surrender to Babylon; Tzidkiyahu wavers, fears his own nobles, and fails to act on YHWH's word; his eyes are gouged out after he watches his sons killed.
The nobles have Yirmeyahu thrown into a muddy cistern to die; Eved-Melekh, an Ethiopian official in the king's house, intervenes with the king's permission, pulls Yirmeyahu out with ropes and rags.

An Ethiopian (Kushite) eunuch in King Tzidkiyahu's court who rescued Yirmeyahu from the cistern; YHWH later promises Eved-Melekh specifically: 'I will deliver you in that day; you shall not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid.'

Yirmeyahu 39 records the fall of Yerushalayim: Babylonian commanders enter the middle gate; Tzidkiyahu flees and is captured; his sons are killed before his eyes; his eyes are gouged out; he is taken to Babylon.

The narrative of the final siege captures the desperate situation of a city under siege, with Yirmeyahu counseling surrender while nobles accuse him of weakening morale; the city falls after the siege breaks into the city.

Yirmeyahu 33:20 — YHWH's covenant with David and the Levites is as unbreakable as the covenant with day and night: 'If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time...' — only then can YHWH's covenant be broken.

faq.question: Why did Yirmeyahu buy a field during the siege?
faq.answer: Buying a field during a siege is an absurd act by any calculation — the city is about to fall. That is precisely the sign's power: YHWH instructed Yirmeyahu to make the purchase as a prophetic declaration that the exile is not the end. Deeds are signed, witnesses gathered, and the records stored in an earthen jar — 'for thus says YHWH: houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land.'

faq.question: What is the Covenant of Day and Night in Yirmeyahu 33?
faq.answer: In Yirmeyahu 33:20-26, YHWH grounds the Davidic covenant and the Levitical covenant in the reliability of the natural order. If the cycle of day and night could be broken, only then could YHWH's covenant with David be broken. No human failure breaks it because YHWH's covenant is as embedded in creation as the rotation of the earth.

faq.question: Who was Eved-Melekh and why is he significant?
faq.answer: Eved-Melekh (meaning 'Servant of the King') was an Ethiopian (Kushite) eunuch in King Tzidkiyahu's court. When the nobles threw Yirmeyahu in a muddy cistern to die, Eved-Melekh intervened: he got permission from the king, took men and rags, and pulled Yirmeyahu out with ropes before he died. YHWH specifically promised Eved-Melekh deliverance on the day of Yerushalayim's fall because he trusted in YHWH.

faq.question: Why did Tzidkiyahu fail to follow YHWH's word through Yirmeyahu?
faq.answer: Tzidkiyahu consulted Yirmeyahu privately, believed YHWH's word enough to ask again and again, but was paralyzed by fear of his own nobles and of the Judahites who had already defected to Babylon. He could not act against the political pressure. Yirmeyahu pleads with him directly in 38:20: 'Please obey the voice of YHWH in what I say to you, and it will go well with you and your life will be spared.' Tzidkiyahu chose the nobles' fear over YHWH's word.

faq.question: What is the significance of Yerushalayim's fall in chapter 39?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 39 records the fulfillment of everything Yirmeyahu had been prophesying for decades: Babylonian commanders enter the city, Tzidkiyahu flees, is caught, watches his sons executed, has his eyes put out, and is led to Babylon in chains. The Temple is burned, the walls broken down, and the people exiled. The prophecy of the boiling pot from the north (chapter 1) has arrived.

faq.question: What does Yirmeyahu 32:17 pray and what does YHWH answer?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu's prayer in 32:17 begins with the act of creation — 'you made the heavens and the earth... nothing is too hard for you' — and then struggles with the apparent contradiction: YHWH commanded him to buy a field, but YHWH also said the city will fall. YHWH's answer (32:27): 'Behold, I am YHWH, the Creator of all flesh. Is anything too hard for me?' The question is rhetorical — YHWH can both judge and restore.

faq.question: What is the significance of the two deed copies in Yirmeyahu 32?
faq.answer: One deed was sealed (private record) and one open (public record), both stored in an earthen jar for safekeeping during the exile. The careful legal protocol — weighing silver, signing witnesses, following the customary deed procedures — during a siege makes the sign more powerful. Yirmeyahu follows the full legal process for a land purchase that he will never be able to use, because the land purchase points beyond his own life to future restoration.

faq.question: How did the nobles' accusation against Yirmeyahu in Yirmeyahu 38:4 reveal their own situation?
faq.answer: The nobles charge Yirmeyahu with 'weakening the hands of the soldiers' by telling them to surrender — a capital offense. The irony is that the city's situation is already desperate, and Yirmeyahu's counsel to surrender is YHWH's word for how to save lives. The nobles silence the prophet because his truth exposes their failed resistance; they are more afraid of his words than of Babylon's armies.

faq.question: What does the rescue of Yirmeyahu by an Ethiopian official reveal?
faq.answer: Eved-Melekh the Kushite acts when no Yehudite stands up for Yirmeyahu. His intervention is recorded in detail — the rags under the ropes, the careful plan — because YHWH honors it specifically with an individual promise of deliverance. This is a repeated pattern in Yirmeyahu: an outsider (here, an Ethiopian) recognizes and honors YHWH's word when YHWH's own people reject it.

faq.question: What is the theological statement of Yirmeyahu 33:3?
faq.answer: 'Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known.' Given to Yirmeyahu while he is imprisoned during the siege, this promise reaffirms that prayer still works even when the city is falling. YHWH is accessible and responsive; there are things still to be revealed even in the darkest moment. The 'hidden things' (betzurot) refers to things inaccessible to human knowledge — YHWH alone can reveal them.

faq.question: Why is the Righteous Branch prophecy in Yirmeyahu 33 significant alongside chapter 23?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 33:15-16 repeats the Righteous Branch promise from 23:5-6 with a twist: in 23, the Branch is named 'YHWH Our Righteousness'; in 33:16, the city of Yerushalayim itself is called by that name. This expands the promise: not only a coming Davidic ruler but the city and community itself will embody YHWH's righteousness. The covenant promise permeates the whole restored community.
